body.text: Key Points
• A lawsuit accusing seven Cornell fraternity members of a 2024 gang rape has reopened a criminal case that ended without charges.
• Online, an "I am Jane Doe" campaign protecting the accuser is being likened to #MeToo.
This article contains references to sexual violence.
Allegations that a student was drugged and raped by members of a Cornell University fraternity have led women in the United States and beyond to post the words "I am Jane Doe" online.
The campaign has drawn comparisons with the #MeToo movement of almost a decade ago.

The former Cornell student, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit in the New York Supreme Court last month. She alleges seven current and former members of the university's Chi Phi fraternity sexually assaulted her over several hours at their fraternity house in October 2024.
The allegations have not been tested in court, and no criminal charges were laid in 2024.

Since the lawsuit was filed, a criminal case has been reopened, and New York governor Kathy Hochul has appointed the state's attorney general Letitia James as special prosecutor. James has described it as "an active criminal investigation".
Jane Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, told CNN on Monday she has "received multiple threats" of harm unless she withdraws her lawsuit.

Dr Rachael Burgin, a senior lecturer at Swinburne University and CEO of Rape and Sexual Assault Research and Advocacy, said the case has exposed how endemic sexual violence is within US fraternity culture, and how long it has gone unchallenged.
"It's notorious for sexual violence … [and] violence generally; hazing rituals, a lot of antisocial, violent, dangerous behaviour, including, and in particular, against women and girls," she said.
"That goes ignored, it's taken young people and students standing up to say, 'Hey, this isn't right'."
What the lawsuit alleges
The lawsuit was first reported on 18 September by Cereese Qusba of Cornell's student newspaper, The Cornell Daily Sun.
Lawyers for Lopes, Kretzschmar and Norris have denied the allegations against their clients. The other men have not commented publicly.

According to the lawsuit, Jane Doe was a 20-year-old student living in the Tri Delta sorority house. At around 11pm on 19 October 2024, having drunk about 10 standard drinks in three hours, she walked alone to the Chi Phi house to see a friend, Ingalls.

After they danced, Ingalls allegedly proposed a threesome with another fraternity brother. The lawsuit states that "in her drunken state, [the] Plaintiff was incapable of consenting to this proposition".

It alleges Ingalls and Newell then pressured her into snorting what they said was ketamine, a drug she had never taken. They also allegedly gave her marijuana and high-proof liquor before engaging in sexual acts without her consent. A third man, Lopes, allegedly joined them later.

At 1.42am, while the alleged assault was under way, Newell allegedly posted in "Chi Phi Actives", a Snapchat group for the chapter's active members, that there was "free p---y" upstairs. CBS News has reported the group chat included 57 men.

As multiple members came into the room, Jane Doe "retreated under the covers of the bed, to hide her naked body from the fraternity men", the lawsuit said. With her phone across the room, she felt there was "no way for her to escape this room full of predatory, fraternity men".

The lawsuit alleges the seven men then snorted lines of ketamine off her body. Two of them allegedly took her to a smaller room, believed to be the fraternity president's office. There, she said, she was assaulted again until around 5.45am, when she lost consciousness.
She reported the incident to Cornell University Police in November 2024. Her lawyer said she later left the university.
Cornell and prosecutors under scrutiny
Cornell temporarily suspended the chapter and the seven men. The lawsuit claims they were "afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays to Cornell".

In a 28 September statement, Cornell said none of the men were offered essays "as a sole consequence of their involvement", and that a Title IX panel had issued expulsions and suspensions. CBS News reports the university has said two were expelled, two were suspended, one had graduated, and two were found not responsible for sexual misconduct.
Chi Phi said the chapter removed the accused within three days of her police report and later permanently expelled them.

Tompkins County district attorney Matthew Van Houten has said Jane Doe's original statement to campus police described her participation as "voluntary, conscious, and consensual". Her lawyer disputes that.

Van Houten has said his office relied on the campus police investigation. He told the BBC he received only a short, signed statement from Jane Doe and a screenshot of the Snapchat messages, and never saw the transcript of her interviews with campus police.

CBS News New York obtained that transcript. It reported that she told police of the initial encounter: "I was pretty OK with all of this." Of what happened later that night, she said: "I can say with 100 per cent confidence I was raped."
Hochul has said she "will not allow anyone to sweep this case under the rug", and Cornell has agreed to an independent review.

The case comes after Cornell's own 2025 survey found 35 per cent of undergraduate women had experienced non consensual sexual contact involving force or incapacitation since starting at the university.
A movement in the making

The "I am Jane Doe" posts began after a political commentator publicly called for the woman to be identified. As with #MeToo, many women are pairing the phrase with their own experiences of sexual violence.
"People are trying to dox this victim-survivor, and they (the posters) are trying to protect her," said Burgin, whose organisation advocates for victim-survivors of sexual violence.
"Everybody knows a victim-survivor, but nobody knows a rapist."

Burgin sees the campaign as an extension of #MeToo. In her view, it draws on the same "collective consciousness raising" on social media and moves conversations women have long had in private onto a global stage.
"We're fed up with the reactions and responses of institutions," she said.
The transparency of US civil courts has given the case its reach, she said, by putting the alleged events in detail on the public record.
In Australia, suppression orders routinely keep that kind of detail from view.
With young Australians consuming so much American content on social media, the case has come to feel close to home.
"We see news coming from America like it is local," Burgin said.
